subject: science
passage: In 1993, a small study reported that college students who listened to a Mozart sonata for ten minutes scored better on a spatial reasoning task than students who sat in silence. News reports soon claimed that Mozart's music could make listeners smarter, and some parents began playing classical music to their babies.
passage_b: Later studies told a more modest story. When researchers repeated the experiment, any improvement was small and lasted only minutes. It also appeared after people listened to other music they enjoyed, suggesting that a good mood, not Mozart in particular, briefly sharpened their thinking.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claims in the news reports in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that the effect was brief and was not special to Mozart's music
choices.B: By claiming that listening to music has no effect at all on thinking
choices.C: By agreeing that Mozart's music has a lasting effect on intelligence
choices.D: By arguing that babies benefit more from music than college students do

explanation.why: Text 1 says news reports claimed Mozart "could make listeners smarter." Text 2 says the improvement "was small and lasted only minutes" and also followed "other music they enjoyed." So Text 2 would answer that the effect was short-lived and not unique to Mozart.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 reports that the effect was brief and also appeared with other enjoyable music.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says a good mood "briefly sharpened their thinking," so it does not deny every effect.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says any improvement "lasted only minutes," so it was not lasting.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Neither text compares the effects of music on babies and on college students.
